item.title: Before and after: Satellite images show Southwest flood destruction - LeadStory
item.summary: Satellite images show Pagosa Springs, Colorado, and Farmington and Flora Vista, New Mexico, before and after flooding from the San Juan and Animas ...
item.page_text:
Satellite imagery has documented the significant damage caused by severe flooding in the US Southwest, particularly affecting Pagosa Springs, Colorado, and Farmington, New Mexico. The San Juan and Animas Rivers both overflowed, resulting in the transformation of dry terrain into muddy expanses and the disappearance of roads.

Hundreds of homes in Colorado and New Mexico have been damaged due to the storms and flooding. According to NOAA, the Four Corners region has received over 20 trillion gallons of rain in the past two weeks, contributing to the historic flooding.

item.title: Taking a Gander at Utah’s Goosenecks
item.summary: The San Juan River has carved deep, improbably curvy meanders into the desert landscape.
item.page_text:
The San Juan River has carved deep, improbably curvy meanders into the desert landscape.
Tens of millions of years ago, the San Juan River in what is now southern Utah shared some characteristics with today's Mississippi River. In a bygone geologic era, the San Juan flowed across a relatively flat plain that formed in an ancient marine environment. Unencumbered by rugged terrain, the river was free to take a long, meandering path on its gradual journey downslope.
But this part of the San Juan changed when geologic forces pushed the Colorado Plateau upward. Some experts think that within the later stages of this “ still-enigmatic ” history, starting around 20 million years ago, the plateau’s rise elevated the San Juan’s headwaters , which increased the river’s gradient and sped its flow. With that, the water’s erosive power intensified, and the river started carving its winding path deeper and deeper through 300-million-year-old rock.
Today, on its westward path to Lake Powell, the San Juan River flows through an impressive series of entrenched meanders, also known as “goosenecks.” An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed the stark desert topography on October 6, 2026.
In Utah’s Goosenecks State Park , the river runs through a canyon 1,000 feet (300 meters) deep. In places, it nearly loops back on itself, making horseshoe-shaped bends. One section is so curvy that the river travels 5.5 miles (8.9 kilometers) between two points that are only 1.3 miles (2.1 kilometers) apart as the crow—nay, goose—flies.
While the goosenecks are an unusual geologic wonder to behold by day, the area’s dark skies are a spectacle by night. Goosenecks State Park’s remote, high-desert location and 360-degree views of the sky helped earn it an International Dark Sky Park designation in 2021. According to DarkSky International, features such as the Double Cluster in Perseus and the Messier 24 star cloud in the Sagittarius spiral arm of the Milky Way are visible to the unaided eye from the park. In November 2026 , dark skies offer the chance to view several meteor showers, with the Northern Taurids, Southern Taurids, and Leonids reaching their peaks throughout the month.
Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-188830 was acquired on October 6, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 400 millimeters. It is provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The image was taken by a member of the Expedition 75 crew. The image has been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed. The International Space Station Program supports the laboratory as part of the ISS National Lab to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the internet. Additional images taken by astronauts and cosmonauts can be viewed at the NASA/JSC Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth . Photo by Bob Wick (BLM) , via Flickr. Story by Lindsey Doermann.

item.title: A lost sea channel shaped this striking corner of Cyprus - Earth.com
item.summary: ... Seasonal rains begin replenishing Akrotiri Salt Lake on Cyprus's southern coast in this Landsat 8 image. Credit: NASA Earth ...
item.page_text:
A satellite image of Cyprus reveals how ancient islands joined to form the Akrotiri Peninsula, enclosing a salt lake once open to the sea.
A shallow salt lake at the southern edge of Cyprus marks a place where the Mediterranean once flowed between two islands.
Today, strips of land join those islands together, leaving a coastal landscape that still carries the outline of its watery past.
The Akrotiri Peninsula offers a striking reminder that even an island’s shape is temporary.
Rivers, shifting shorelines, and rising rock helped build this southern tip of Cyprus, connecting land that once stood apart.
On October 10, 2026, Landsat 8 captured images of the peninsula’s sandy margins and the lake enclosed between them.
Behind that modern view lies a story spanning ancient ocean floors, migrating flamingos, and a cape whose name recalls a legendary arrival of cats.
Akrotiri Salt Lake occupies a former arm of the Mediterranean.
Its enclosure happened gradually, as sediment accumulated along two routes between Cyprus and a smaller island to the south.
These natural connections are known as tombolos: deposits of sand, gravel, or other sediment that link an island to another landmass.
At Akrotiri, two such bridges helped turn separate islands into a single peninsula.
The western connection formed first. About 50,000 years ago, gravel and sand delivered by the Kouris River began building the tombolo on that side.
The eastern connection developed later, extending south from Cyprus.
Geologists place the final separation of the lagoon from the open Mediterranean within the past 2,000 years.
That difference in timing gives the landscape an unusual perspective.
Although the rocks beneath Cyprus record tens of millions of years, the closure that helped define this lake occurred within human history.
The two land bridges also explain why the lake sits where it does. Rather than forming in an isolated inland basin, it occupies space left between growing coastal connections.
Its position preserves evidence of the channel even though the surrounding land now provides an unbroken route onto the peninsula.
Long before those sediment bridges formed, the material that would become Cyprus was taking shape underwater.
About 90 million years ago, during the Late Cretaceous, molten rock emerged from the seafloor and cooled into new oceanic crust.
Tectonic forces eventually pushed portions of that crust upward, bringing formerly submerged rock above the waves.
The Troodos Mountains preserve remnants of this ancient oceanic material.
Geologists call the rock assemblage an ophiolite, a term associated with the snakelike appearance of some of its mottled green rocks.
The peninsula’s southern portion has a different geological background.
During the much later Miocene epoch, marine deposits accumulated around the emerging island, including chalk, limestone, and marl.
Later uplift raised some of this younger material into a smaller island offshore.
River sediment and marine deposits eventually filled parts of the intervening channel, creating the connections visible in the peninsula’s present shape.
The lake now follows a seasonal rhythm. Water typically returns in late autumn and winter, while summer brings drying.
Those winter waters have historically supported large gatherings of flamingos , with overwintering numbers averaging about 4,000 birds.
The birds come to feed on small creatures such as fairy shrimp. These shrimp contain carotenoids, pigments that contribute to the flamingos’ familiar pink coloration.
Recent counts offer a more sobering picture. News reports put the lake’s wintering flamingo population at just 30 birds in 2025, a sharp departure from its historical abundance.
The satellite scene captures the setting for this seasonal gathering.
The birds themselves, and the changes in their numbers, belong to a smaller scale of observation that adds another layer to the landscape’s story.
On the southeastern peninsula, Cape Gata introduces a different animal connection. Its name means Cape Cat in Greek.
According to legend, a severe fourth-century drought left Cyprus struggling with snakes. Empress Helena, the mother of Constantine the Great, responded by arranging for cats to arrive from Egypt.
The story places some of those cats near what became the Holy Monastery of St. Nicholas of the Cats, where monks supposedly encouraged them to hunt snakes.
The tale survives alongside a continuing tradition of caring for cats at the monastery.
Seen together, the lake, land bridges, and cape reveal several histories sharing one small stretch of coast.
Ancient seabed became an island, sediment closed a channel, and people attached stories to the land that emerged.
The shoreline in this image is the latest chapter in a landscape still shaped by water.

item.title: How Online Maps Lay Bare the US Military Bases Targeted by Iran
item.summary: Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published. Become a member and support our work here. In September, CBS News obtained new images of the aftermath of attacks on US bases in the Middle East from active service members. One told the news channel: “This is major […]
item.page_text:
Sebastian is a researcher at Bellingcat, specialising in terrorism and civilian harm in conflict. He has investigated violence and human rights abuses in the Middle East and West Africa. He previously worked at BBC Verify, the Centre for Information Resilience, and the International Criminal Court.
Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published . Become a member and support our work here .
In September, CBS News obtained new images of the aftermath of attacks on US bases in the Middle East from active service members. One told the news channel : “This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public. “We’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face,” they added.
While reports have detailed how Iran used Russian intelligence , including satellite imagery , to identify US troops, ships and aircraft, Bellingcat found that publicly available mapping platforms also reveal detailed and potentially sensitive information about US military bases in the Middle East.
Google Maps and other online mapping services contain dozens of labels identifying facilities including headquarters, accommodation, gyms and fuel points. Publicly available photographs and videos, including material published by the US military, provide further details about how these facilities are used.
Experts told Bellingcat that such information could have helped inform Iranian targeting decisions by revealing where personnel gather and how bases operate. However, they cautioned that Iran would also have had access to other sources of intelligence. Reporting from Reuters earlier this year also highlighted how US officials believed commercially available location data was being used to target US troops in war zones.
The bases examined by Bellingcat are not secret and have operated for years in a region where US forces maintained a strong sense of security. Joseph Jarnecki, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute , said the US had been able to maintain aerial superiority and was understood to have significant air defence capabilities, but that Iran’s missile and drone campaign has undermined both assumptions.
Iranian strikes have damaged at least 20 US military sites across Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq and Saudi Arabia since the conflict began in February this year.
Governments can request that Google blur or remove sensitive information from its services and Google publishes data on government requests for content removal.
Bellingcat contacted the US Department of Defense who asked us to reach out to CENTCOM about the details in this story. We also contacted Google. However, we did not receive responses to questions from these respondents before publication.
We examined four of the largest and most heavily affected US military installations by Iran’s missile and drone campaign: Camp Buehring and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait, Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan and Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. At each one, we found publicly available Google Maps information providing details about facilities inside the bases and how they are used.
At Camp Buehring in Kuwait, Google Maps identifies what is labelled as the main headquarters building, as well as a gym and a self-help facility, all of which were among locations destroyed by recent Iranian strikes. In addition to Google Maps place markers there are dozens of reviews and user-uploaded photographs.
Bellingcat verified that this was a headquarters building by matching the flagpoles and layout in a photo published by the US military’s Defense Visual Information Distribution Service (DVIDS) showing soldiers posing in front of the  building to the Google Maps satellite image.
We also identified details about one of the camp’s gyms, including the building’s layout and roof structure, as well as Google reviews that indicate when it is busiest.
Among the images published by CBS News in September was that of a heavily damaged tent-like structure with smoke rising from it. Bellingcat matched the location of this image to the above satellite imagery, verifying that it shows the gym building pinned on Google Maps.
⚡️🚨 Exclusive images released showing damage to E-3 Sentry AWACS aircraft at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, plus damage to US military camps Arifjan and Buehring in Kuwait from Iranian strikes. Images sent to CBS by active US military personnel. (IRIB News) https://t.co/1urA44f4xz
A building labeled on Google as “DPW Self-Help Center” was also destroyed at Camp Buehring. Its Google Maps listing includes opening hours, and a photo posted by a Master Sergeant in 2017 labeled “ My office in Kuwait ” shows the interior of an office. Some of the notices on the walls inside the office are legible, including what appears to be a floor plan.
A Google Maps placemark labelled “ Transient Tent ” identifies a large accommodation area, while another review includes a ground-level photograph of one of the tents. The dining facility can also be seen from the inside, including information regarding meal times .
William Goodhind of Contested Ground , a visual forensics consultancy that uses OSINT and satellite imagery to analyse military sites, said the information available on Google Maps could reveal “the camp’s layout, the division between secure and non-secure areas, confirms likely accommodation areas, and shows day/time periods of low and high activity.”
A satellite image of Kuwait’s Camp Arifjan, captured by Planet on March 4, 2026 and published by the The Washington Post , shows damage to numerous structures at the base. Bellingcat compared the image with publicly available mapping data to identify two damaged facilities.

item.title: Creek Fire Snow Persistence GeoAI - Mohammadreza Narimani
item.summary: ... GeoAI . Frontiers in Forests and Global Change 9:2016172 (2026)—read and cite the open-access paper.
item.page_text:
Parastoo Farajpoor and Mohammadreza Narimani * (corresponding author)
Frontiers in Forests and Global Change · Volume 9 · Article 2016172 · 4 November 2026 · Open access CC BY
Department of Biological and Agricultural Engineering · University of California, Davis
Mountain snow links forest condition to the timing and availability of water across the western United States. Warming is already changing snow amount, duration, and seasonality, while wildfire increasingly overlaps Sierra Nevada landscapes that historically retained snow through winter and spring. For hydrologists, forest managers, and remote-sensing researchers searching for Creek Fire snow persistence , post-fire snowpack , or wildfire severity and snow , the practical question is not only “can we map snow after fire?” but “did fire change snow relative to comparable unburned terrain?”
Canopy removal can reduce interception and increase the fraction of snowfall reaching the ground, yet it also changes shading, longwave radiation, wind, and redistribution. Char on snow can lower albedo and accelerate melt. The same burned landscape can therefore show both greater accumulation and faster ablation. Satellite snow cover, snow disappearance date, snow depth, and snow water equivalent describe related but different quantities—so a high machine-learning score on one optical metric does not automatically prove a causal fire effect.
This open-access Frontiers study by Parastoo Farajpoor and Mohammadreza Narimani (corresponding author, University of California, Davis) builds an explainable multisource GeoAI framework for seasonal snow persistence after the 2020 Creek Fire . The analysis uses Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel-2 (HLS) observations for eleven water years (WY2016–WY2026) on a 500 m grid, matched before–after control–impact (BACI) comparisons, and spatially blocked machine learning with SHAP attribution.
The workflow separates four tasks that are often conflated in wildfire remote sensing: (1) constructing a seasonal optical snow-persistence metric from HLS; (2) classifying spectral burn severity with Sentinel-2 dNBR; (3) estimating fire-associated change with matched BACI contrasts; and (4) asking whether terrain, climate, and fire descriptors can predict raw persistence versus the fire-adjusted anomaly under spatial cross-validation.
Seasonal persistence is defined as the fraction of clear-sky HLS observations classified as snow between 1 October and 30 July of each water year. Snow classification uses NDSI with green reflectance thresholds on Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 collections. That metric tracks how often snow is optically detectable under clear skies—it is not snow water equivalent, and it is not the fraction of calendar days with snow.
The 2020 Creek Fire burned roughly 1,544 km² in California’s central Sierra Nevada, overlapping montane forests with substantial pre-existing drought- and bark-beetle-associated tree mortality. Five pre-fire and six post-fire snow seasons allow the post-fire record to be interpreted against both local baselines and contemporaneous unburned controls.
Candidate controls were drawn from a 5–30 km annulus beyond the perimeter: the inner buffer reduces boundary mixing, while the outer limit keeps a regional comparison pool. Geographic proximity alone was not treated as evidence of comparability. Matching used terrain and pre-fire snow conditions so that treatment and control cells start from similar physical settings before the fire year.
Eligible snow-zone cells required mean pre-fire persistence greater than 0.05, yielding 3,778 perimeter-internal treatment cells matched to unburned controls. Absolute standardized mean differences after matching were no greater than 0.047 , indicating strong covariate balance on the matching variables.
Elevation, slope, northness, and Sentinel-2 dNBR classes structure the burned landscape. Raw post-minus-pre persistence maps show where optical snow detection changed, but those raw maps are not control-adjusted: both burned and unburned cells can move together when climate varies from year to year. That is why the BACI design is central to claims about fire-associated change.
Across all matched cells, the landscape-average BACI contrast was only +0.0017 , with a year-level 95% confidence interval from −0.023 to +0.027 (p = 0.88). Both treatment and matched-control cells increased in mean persistence after the fire; their similar movement is why the adjusted contrast is much smaller than a naive before–after difference inside the perimeter.
A clearer signal appears in the highest dNBR class (≥0.44; n = 448): the BACI contrast was +0.026 (2.6 percentage points), with a year-level interval of +0.002 to +0.050 and about 66% positive cell-level contrasts. Moderate severity showed a smaller positive contrast (+0.007); low-severity and internal low-change classes were not distinguishable from zero at the year level. Severity therefore identifies a class-level optical snow response more clearly than a strong, uniformly graded cell-level relationship (Spearman ρ between continuous dNBR and cell BACI ≈ 0.11).
Annual spatial agreement between HLS and MODIS persistence was high throughout the eleven-season record (mean Pearson r = 0.947 ; range 0.912–0.970). Both products captured the same prominent annual contrasts, including the low-persistence WY2018 season and the high-persistence WY2023 season. HLS domain means were often slightly higher than MODIS, but the shared pattern supports using HLS as a consistent optical snow indicator for this GeoAI study.
Under 5 km spatial-block cross-validation , XGBoost predicted raw post-fire persistence with out-of-fold R² = 0.811 . The same model family applied to the fire-adjusted anomaly reached only R² = 0.046 . In other words, environmental-state prediction can look excellent while disturbance-response prediction remains weak—exactly the distinction researchers need when searching for “explainable GeoAI wildfire snow” or

item.summary: The new map shows trend in the right direction for southern, central and eastern Utah. All areas have seen improvements, and few isolated spots ...
item.page_text:
SALT LAKE CITY, Utah — Recent heavy rainfall and flooding over the past few weeks has provided a silver lining in the drought situation across the state. With the new Drought Monitor Map being released for this week, very positive trends can be seen.
Coming out of the summer, most of the state was under Extreme Drought conditions. Even through the middle of October, several spots across the state were dealing with moderate to extreme conditions.
The new map shows trend in the right direction for southern, central and eastern Utah.  All areas have seen improvements, and few isolated spots through northeastern Utah are no longer under drought conditions.
Michael Sanchez from Utah Division of Water Resources explains that it's been several months since we've seen some parts of Utah under no drought concerns.
"The last time we saw zero drought in parts of the state was in June 2025, and 3% of the state was in zero," Sanchez said.
He also cautions the state to not let up on conservation efforts. Even though high water use is sustained through the summer months, our indoor water use can be minimized by taking shorter baths and showers and implement more water efficient appliances.

item.page_text:
By clicking Continue to join or sign in, you agree to LinkedIn’s User Agreement , Privacy Policy , and Cookie Policy .
For Day 5 of #30DayMapChallenge : Sight, I've done a viewshed analysis for wind turbines in Nolan and Taylor counties in Texas and mapped it with Mapbox . 

This one was a really interesting research project leading to some new features in mapgl.

On the map, the colors show how many turbine blade tips are in line of sight from each spot on the ground, out to 25 miles. 

Zoom in and the turbines appear as 3D models, built in Blender and scaled to their real size, using new 3D model support in R's mapgl package.

Viewshed rasters were pre-computed in R with terra and pulled in on turbine click.  Estimated visibility comes from Argonne National Laboratory field research on how far away wind facilities stand out.

The observer is the blade tip, the target is a person's eye about 5.6 feet above the ground, and the calculation corrects for Earth's curvature and atmospheric refraction. Elevation comes from USGS 3DEP.

All of this month's maps are here: https://lnkd.in/gmhMJupH .  Give this one a look and definitely try making your own 3D models and mapping them with mapgl.
Viewshed is a great fit for 'Sight'. Did you model hub height and blade tip separately? I'd be curious how much the visible area changes between the two.

item.title: Super El Niño nearing a record, and the weather pattern looks like it
item.summary: This map shows rankings of mean temperatures for fall 2026 through Nov. 4. Locations with a dark brown box labeled "1" had a record warm Sept. 1 ...
item.page_text:
The current super El Niño is nearing record strength and is already showing its effects on the nation's weather, from flooding rain to a warm and dry fall.
Water temperatures near the equator in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean region meteorologists monitor for El Niño were 2.5 degrees Celsius above average as of the last week of October.
This animation shows sea-surface temperature anomalies from late April through the end of October 2026. The El Niño shows up in the middle of the map near the equator in the Pacific Ocean.
Based on daily data using an old "oceanic Niño index" (ONI), it would be a new all-time record.
However, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center officially uses data averaged over three-month periods and a new index that filters out the surrounding warming ocean from climate change called the "relative oceanic Niño index" (RONI).
Their latest three-month RONI value from August through October (1.97 degrees above average) is a little behind the pace from the 1997 (2.07 degrees) El Niño.
Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value.
The record three-month RONI in NOAA's database was 2.4 degrees above average from December 1982 through February 1983.
This graph shows three-month values of the relative sea-surface temperature anomalies in degrees Celsius in the Niño3.4 region, the area of the equatorial Pacific Ocean monitored for El Niño. The red line depicts the 2026 values, which reached the El Niño threshold in the May-July period. The red arrow shows the August-October anomaly while the brown arrow shows the record in NOAA's database set from December 1982 through February 1983.
NOAA uses longer-term data to filter out short-term changes in the weather and ocean from the El Niño signal, according to James Belanger, The Weather Company vice president of meteorology.
Regardless, the NOAA latest monthly outlook says chances "remain high for a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950."
Based on past intense El Niño events and on the current pace, that record could be reached some time late this fall or early winter.
Climate scientist Zeke Hausfather pointed out this El Niño is likely to be the strongest in 1,000 years , based on evidence from tree rings and ocean corals.
The stronger the El Niño, the more certain it will impact the weather pattern.
It has already done that, limiting the Atlantic hurricane season to only one hurricane, the fewest on record since 1925.
And it now appears the typical winter impacts of El Niño have already started to settle in over the U.S. 1 to 2 months early , according to meteorologist and El Niño expert Eric Webb.
This map shows the typical winter pattern over the U.S. and Canada during an El Niño.
In the past couple of weeks, we've had two major flash flood events in the Desert Southwest , followed by up to 2 feet of rain inundating parts of the Florida Peninsula and a major overnight flash flood in the mountains of northern Georgia and southeastern Tennessee.
According to the Southeast Regional Climate Center , it's been a record wet fall through Nov. 4 in Albuquerque (5.20 inches), Flagstaff, Arizona (13.15 inches) and West Palm Beach, Florida (34.68 inches).
Elsewhere, it has been very warm and mainly dry.
Dozens of cities in the central U.S. have had a record warm fall through early November, including Chicago, Dallas, Houston and Nashville, according to the SERCC.
This map shows rankings of mean temperatures for fall 2026 through Nov. 4. Locations with a dark brown box labeled "1" had a record warm Sept. 1 through Nov. 4 period.
So, while the daily and weekly weather may throw a few curveballs as usual, this warm North, wet South pattern is forecast to last at least through February.
Jonathan Erdman is a senior meteorologist at weather.com and has been covering national and international weather since 1996. Extreme and bizarre weather are his favorite topics. Reach out to him on Bluesky , X (formerly Twitter) and Facebook .

item.title: Introducing the Planet AI App: Search. Explore. Act.
item.summary: Search the planet using everyday language and explore a decade of near-daily satellite imagery with no GIS expertise required.
item.page_text:
See what you can discover. Sign up and start exploring at ai.planet.com.
AI chat apps are now incredibly adept at answering our questions about human knowledge. But for all their power, they are fundamentally blind to the physical world. If a farmer asks how to improve their crop yield, a chatbot will give the agricultural theory but know nothing about their field today. Same for a first responder facing a flood or a journalist investigating a landslide.
In short, today’s chatbots live only in the digital world. That’s why I’m excited to share that my team at Planet has built an application that takes the power of the AI chat app into the physical domain.
The new Planet AI app lets users search ten years of Planet imagery to find sites of interest, explore how they’ve changed over time, and contextualize what they find with publicly available information, all in a simple, map-based chat interface. Locally and globally. Through space and through time. Beginning today, anyone can use this tool to explore their hunches and messy questions using everyday language.
This summer, hundreds of users tried an early version of the app, and we learned a lot from their experience. Perhaps most notably, we learned that many of them really liked using the tool in the discovery phase of their work, when they were determining where to search or start their analysis.
One user told us they'd never scroll across an entire desert by hand, so without a tool like this, certain searches simply wouldn’t happen. Another said that AI could help point their team in the right direction and save time. So we built recent enhancements in the app around what’s needed at the beginning of an analysis.
Our AI-enabled search accelerates this initial phase of geospatial analysis with several key capabilities:
With these core capabilities, our AI app democratizes access to geospatial insights, allowing you to minimize the time needed to turn a hunch into a question — or even a hypothesis.
Some of the most compelling early uses of the app have focused on environmental protection and land stewardship.
Conservation teams are testing the tool to monitor vast habitats, spot illegal encroachment or fire threats, and verify automated deforestation alerts with imagery before deploying field patrols. By pairing conversational search with time-series comparisons, analysts can track vegetation recovery over time and isolate comparable baseline habitats to prove conservation impact to stakeholders.
Meanwhile, environmental compliance teams demonstrated that they can use AI-enabled search to locate and prioritize industrial sites across entire counties based on proximity to waterways. Workflows that historically took days of manual GIS scanning can now surface high-priority inspection targets in minutes — giving frontline teams the clear visual evidence they need to act fast.
For most of Planet’s history, getting value from our data entailed understanding how to analyze it. AI-enabled search removes this barrier by making it easier to explore and benefit from our archive. It’s part of a bigger idea we call Planetary Intelligence : pairing daily satellite imagery with AI to deliver powerful insights about our changing planet in near-real time, to help life on Earth adapt and thrive.
Today’s AI-enabled search is just the beginning. We look forward to incorporating AI into more of Planet's offerings to help deliver more value for our users. Have an idea about what you’d like to see next? You can use the “share feedback” button on the main menu of the app to share it with us. We welcome your feedback!
It’s easy to get started. Just sign up and start exploring at ai.planet.com . Right now, access is free! Sign in with a Planet Insights account to more easily access premium capabilities in the future.
So go ahead: start exploring those hunches. See what you can discover. When you find something interesting, we encourage you to share it with us or with your community!
